grammar_rules.pattern: Kdybych, kdybys, kdyby, kdybychom, kdybyste, kdyby + -l participle. Word order: kdybych + past participle.
grammar_rules.explanation: Kdyby (if) + conditional forms: Kdybych věděl... (If I knew...), Kdybys chtěl... (If you wanted...), Kdyby přišel... (If he came...). The verb in the kdyby-clause is always in past tense: Kdybych měl čas (If I had time — literally 'if I had had time'). The main clause uses bych + past: šel bych (I would go). This is a complex but essential A2 structure for hypothetical situations. The word order: kdybych + past participle + rest of clause.

grammar_rules.pattern: Abych, abys, aby, abychom, abyste, aby + -l participle. Aby = 'so that / in order to'.
grammar_rules.explanation: 'Aby' introduces purpose clauses — why you do something. It uses the conditional forms + -l participle: Musím se učit, abych udělal zkoušku (I must study so that I pass the exam). Přišel jsem dřív, abychom si mohli popovídat (I came earlier so we could chat). grammar_rules.pattern: Imperfective (process) ↔ Perfective (result) — paired by prefixes: u-, na-, s-/z-, vy-, do-, při-, od-
grammar_rules.explanation: Czech verbs come in aspect pairs: imperfective (ongoing/process) and perfective (completed/result). The perfective is usually formed by adding a prefix to the imperfective. Common prefix patterns: u- (dělat→udělat, vařit→uvařit), na- (psát→napsat, číst→přečíst — note 'na' for writing, 'pře' for reading), s-/z- (dělat→zdělat — rare; more commonly: tvořit→stvořit), vy- (myt→vymýt, brát→vzít), do- (dělat→dodělat, číst→dočíst), při- (nést→přinést), od- (nést→odnést). Not every prefix works with every verb — the pairs must be learned. The key semantic distinction: imperfective answers 'What were you doing?' (psal jsem = I was writing), perfective answers 'What did you do?' (napsal jsem = I wrote [and finished]).

examples.en: to do — process → to do — completed
to write — process → to write — completed
to read — process → to read — completed
to buy — process → to buy — completed

grammar_rules.rule_name: Aspect in context — when to use imperfective vs perfective
grammar_rules.pattern: Imperfective for ongoing/repeated/habitual; perfective for single completed actions with results
grammar_rules.explanation: The choice between imperfective and perfective depends on what you want to communicate. USE IMPERFECTIVE when: describing a process (psal jsem celý večer = I was writing all evening), habitual actions (každý den čtu = I read every day), simultaneous actions (když jsem vařil, ona se dívala = while I was cooking, she was watching), asking 'what were you doing?'. USE PERFECTIVE when: describing a completed action with a result (napsal jsem e-mail = I wrote an email [it's done]), single events (včera jsem koupil auto = yesterday I bought a car), sequential actions (přišel, sedl si a začal číst = he came, sat down, and started reading), asking 'what did you do?'. At A2 level, learners need to RECOGNIZE the distinction — active production is B1.

examples.en: I was writing a letter when she called. (imperfective — process)

examples.cz: Napsal jsem dopis a odeslal ho.
examples.en: I wrote a letter and sent it. (perfective — completed)
Every day I cook lunch. (imperfective — habitual)
Yesterday I cooked svíčková. (perfective — single completed)
